lines: Here is a pointer whose entire job is letting two threads look at the same number at once. Nothing more.
Notice what's missing: no gate, no lock, no permission check anywhere in sight. Sharing and changing turn out to be two completely different privileges.
Take that same pointer and try to write through it directly, from either side, with nothing guarding the access.
Before a single thread even runs, will the compiler let this line exist at all?
answer: No. Counting how many owners exist is a bookkeeping trick; it never grants a path to change what's being counted.
That path has a name of its own, and this pointer was never given it.

lines: Here is the compiler's own answer, and it names the exact missing piece rather than just refusing.
A pointer that only ever hands out a shared view can't suddenly offer a mutable one; that second ability has to come from somewhere else entirely.
Slide a gate inside the same pointer, and send four real threads at it as fast as they'll go.
Every single one of those twenty five thousand increments per thread lands, because only one thread is ever standing inside that gate at any instant.
One of those four threads panics while it's still standing inside the gate, before it ever steps back out.
The next thread to try the gate gets told, plainly, that something went wrong last time — and the number inside is still there to recover on purpose.
Run the identical panic again, but through a different library's gate this time, built on a different promise entirely.
This one never reports trouble at all; the next thread through just finds the number waiting, as if the panic never happened — a deliberate, opposite bet.
A task takes the gate's own receipt, pauses for a moment mid flight, and then tries to use that receipt again once it resumes.
Will the runtime still accept handing this whole task off to run anywhere it likes?
answer: No. That receipt only ever makes sense on the exact thread that issued it, and a pause is exactly where the runtime might move things.
Still holding it at that instant disqualifies everything built around it, not just the receipt itself.

lines: The ordinary gate's receipt names itself directly in the failure — it was never built with a pause like this in mind.
Swap in a gate built specifically to survive that pause, and the identical shape runs clean, printing out exactly what it should.
Sharing a number and guarding a number turned out to be two entirely separate jobs this whole time, never one standing in for the other.
Two different gates made two opposite bets about what a panic should leave behind, and one gate exists for exactly one reason: surviving a pause while it's still held.
